title: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?

posts.topic_title: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?
posts.author: favalora
posts.post_subject: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?
posts.content_md:
Hi - 

Do any of you have pointers to tutorials for creating a hologram that uses the process of: computing a scene, printing out an enlarged version of the hologram, photographing it with a traditional camera, developing the film, and then illuminating the negative?

A friend's father (phyics prof.) told me about doing this many years ago. Of course I would anticipate a very low film resolution, but I am curious if any of you have tried this.

gregg

posts.topic_title: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?
posts.author: Andy
posts.post_subject: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?
posts.content_md:
I don't know if it is possible to print out a hologram. Even if the hologram is up-scaled, the interference patterns may still be too dense for a 600 dpi printer to be able to "capture". I'm sure it could be done however. I'm planning on doing it.

Andy

posts.topic_title: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?
posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.post_subject: DIY Digital Holograms using photo film negative?
posts.content_md:
R. W. Wood's classic text, Physical Optics, from the early 20th century, has an enlarged zone plate pattern in it for just that purpose. 

I recorded some low spatial frquency gratings on the late lamented Kodak Technical Pan film, now out of production. They were not as efficient as the same gratings exposed on Kodak Holographic Film, S0-173, even though both were processed in the Pyrochrome system. (Both films were exposed using a 35 mm camera body without a lens as the film holder.) I'd be curious to trying that Gigabit film mentioned in the link above.

The big stumbling block to doing this would be more like the lens used rather than the film!
